For 1: It's a tricky answer. STEM covers a lot of ground, and what someone identifies as STEM will modify the answer somewhat. However, there are certainly programs out there to facilitate women entering STEM that did not exist until relatively recently. There are more programs in general to facilitate entering STEM, from DO-IT (a UW based initiative for helping those with disabilities) to a myriad of programs such as these:

http://www.worldwidelearn.com/education-articles/15-innovative-initiatives-bringing-women-into-stem.html

Yet, despite these initiatives, fewer women enter STEM (despite careers often considered STEM dominated by women such as nursing) which leads to 2, to which I can only answer I don't know, because we have no closed system in which there is no societal bias with which to compare ours. However, my guess is that, no matter the incentive, this gap will remain.

Here's my educated guess, with some backing:

Women are equally skilled (and, leaning towards more skilled) than their male peers in the fields that underpin STEM:

https://powermore.dell.com/business/study-women-stem-careers/

Despite these higher skills, women chose not to enter STEM. This does not mirror past expansions into traditionally male fields once the opportunity was present, such as nursing or clerical fields, once highly dominated by men and now nearly dominated by women.

Additionally, the majority of women who do enter STEM fields leave. This is probably due to the fact that of those women who do stay beyond their first year in a STEM field, 67% report they do not have a child at home. This reflects statistics showing that the majority of women with children work less than 39 hours a week, and most less than 33. As a great many traditional STEM jobs require full time status, it is unlikely the number of women in STEM jobs will increase as long as hours remain inflexible.

This chart reflects that, somewhat:

http://blog.dcrworkforce.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/percentage-of-stem-workers-by-gender.jpg

The prime motivation in choosing a job for women seems to be the flexibility to work part time, especially in the critical age range of 25 to 35. As long as this is the case, the often inflexibility of STEM will probably prevent women from joining.

The WHY of this is something we can't answer, whether it is societies input on roles, or biological motivators. I tend toward biology, because the number of women who desire to work if they have children hovers around 50%, from decade to decade, regardless of work status. This, compared to very low numbers of men, in private polls, tends to indicate biology; however, it's interesting to note longer guaranteed maternity leave correlates with higher percentages of employed women, though I was not able to find direct correlation in STEM fields in a cursory search.

Social science tends to be almost exclusively based around correlation. This provides an enormous amount of room for people to "prove" whatever they want to prove. Like the article you linked to mentions, the individual who long since suggested there is a major gender bias in STEM comes out with a result "proving" a gender bias in STEM. The individuals who have long since suggested there is no major gender bias in STEM come out with a study "proving" there is no gender bias in STEM.

As the article you linked to mention there's even a "bias" to longer names. People tend to react far more favorable to short names in hiring. The study "proving" a gender bias, whose author's were likely familiar with this peculiarity, chose to use the names Jennifer and John. This immediately shows the results are going to be little more than a loose correlation, and that is just one of countless confounding variables. The insidious part of social science is that this correlation is then presented as causation when published, "Study proves gender bias in STEM."
